lesson.title: From Odometer to Speedometer: Catching Velocity at an Instant
lesson.summary: Instantaneous velocity is the derivative of a position function with respect to time, the limit of average velocity as the time interval shrinks to zero.
lesson.body:
A car's trip odometer tells you how far you traveled and how long it took, so you can compute an average speed for the whole trip. The speedometer, on the other hand, tells you how fast the car is going right now, at this exact instant. That gap between "average over an interval" and "value at an instant" is exactly the gap between average rate of change and instantaneous rate of change, and velocity is simply that idea applied to position over time.

Suppose a particle moves along a line and its position at time t is given by s(t), measured in meters, with t in seconds. Over the time interval from t to t+h, the particle moves from s(t) to s(t+h), so its average velocity on that interval is the difference quotient (s(t+h) minus s(t)) divided by h. Graphically, this is the slope of the secant line connecting the two points (t, s(t)) and (t+h, s(t+h)) on the position versus time graph. This is nothing new: it is the same average rate of change you have already seen for any function, just with position and time as the variables.

Instantaneous velocity at time t is defined as the limit of that average velocity as h shrinks to zero: v(t) equals the limit as h approaches 0 of [s(t+h) minus s(t)] divided by h. This is precisely the derivative definition applied to s, so v(t) = s'(t). As h gets smaller, the secant lines rotate and settle into the tangent line to the position graph at t, and the slope of that tangent line is the instantaneous velocity. Unlike speed, velocity can be negative: a negative value means position is decreasing, so the particle is moving in the negative direction along the line.

Here is a full worked example. Let s(t) = t squared minus 4t plus 3, and find the instantaneous velocity at t = 1. First expand s(1+h): (1+h)^2 - 4(1+h) + 3 = 1 + 2h + h^2 - 4 - 4h + 3. Collecting terms, the constants give 1 - 4 + 3 = 0, the h terms give 2h - 4h = -2h, leaving s(1+h) = h^2 - 2h. Next, s(1) = 1 - 4 + 3 = 0. The difference quotient is [s(1+h) - s(1)] / h = (h^2 - 2h - 0) / h = (h^2 - 2h) / h = h - 2, after dividing every term by h. Taking the limit as h approaches 0 gives h - 2 approaching -2. So v(1) = -2 meters per second.

That negative sign is meaningful, not an error: at t = 1 the particle is moving backward, in the direction of decreasing s, at a rate of 2 meters per second. If you only computed average velocity over some long interval containing t = 1, you might miss this entirely, the same way a road trip's average speed hides the moments when the car was stopped at a light or speeding on the highway.

Notice that the general pattern s(t) = t^2 - 4t + 3 gives v(t) = 2t - 4 for every t, not just t = 1. Right now the only way to find that formula is to repeat the limit computation above for a general t, which is exactly what you would get if you substitute t for 1 in the steps above. This repetition is precisely the tedium that motivates the differentiation rules covered next: instead of re-running a limit argument every time, you will learn shortcuts that turn s(t) = t^2 - 4t + 3 into v(t) = 2t - 4 almost by inspection.
